Alright, the TUI is up and running inside a tmux session named “glint”. I’ve already verified that the initial render looks correct and that the `/help` command displays the expected help text. The next thing I need to confirm is that invoking a slash command didn’t produce any hidden runtime errors that might have been sent to stderr. When I launched the TUI I redirected its stderr to `/tmp/glint-tui-err.log`, so any uncaught exception or warning would end up there.

Given the recent changes I made to the tool‑hint handling (setting `activeToolHintRef.current` synchronously inside `onToolStart` and removing the `useEffect` that updated the ref), I want to make sure those changes didn’t introduce any subtle bugs that only surface after a command is processed. The `/help` command is simple and shouldn’t trigger any tool usage, but it does go through the command parsing pipeline, so it’s a good minimal test.

To inspect the UI state after the command has been processed, I’ll capture the tmux pane output again. A short pause (`sleep 1`) should give the TUI enough time to render any updates that result from handling the command. I’ll then use `tmux capture-pane -p -t glint` and pipe it to `tail -40` so I get the last few lines of the UI, which should include the command prompt, the echoed `/help` input, and the help text. 

Immediately after that, I’ll print a clear marker (`===ERR===`) and dump the last few lines of the error log (`cat /tmp/glint-tui-err.log | tail -5`). This will let me see if anything was written to stderr during the handling of `/help`. If the error log is empty, I can be confident that the recent ref‑sync change didn’t cause any hidden failures.

All of this can be done in a single Bash command, which fits the tool interface I have. I’ll construct the command exactly as:

```
sleep 1; tmux capture-pane -t glint -p | tail -40; echo "===ERR==="; cat /tmp/glint-tui-err.log | tail -5
```

This will pause briefly, capture the UI, separate the output from any potential errors, and give me a concise view of both. I’ll now issue this as a Bash tool call.
